claim: Two mammalian genes, Kcnt1 and Kcnt2, encode pore-forming subunits of Na+-dependent K+ (KNa) channels.
source: Two mammalian genes, Kcnt1 and Kcnt2, encode pore-forming subunits of Na+-dependent K+ (KNa) channels.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the genetic basis of KNa channels, supported by prior research.

claim: Several mutations in Kcnt1 are associated with intellectual disability and childhood epilepsy.
source: Recent work has revealed a critical role of KNa channels in neuronal function, through demonstration that several mutations in Kcnt1 are associated with intellectual disability and childhood epilepsy (Barcia et al., 2012; Heron et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Barcia et al., 2012; Heron et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2014).

claim: KNa channels are expressed in neurons.
source: Yet, despite apparently wide-spread expression both in neurons (Bhattacharjee et al., 2002, 2005) and other cells (Kameyama et al., 1984; Niu and Meech, 2000), the physiological roles of KNa currents during normal patterns of neuronal activity remain poorly understood in part because of the absence of suitably selective pharmacological tools and also the complexities than can arise from manipulations of Na+.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Bhattacharjee et al., 2002, 2005).

claim: KNa channels are expressed in cells other than neurons.
source: Yet, despite apparently wide-spread expression both in neurons (Bhattacharjee et al., 2002, 2005) and other cells (Kameyama et al., 1984; Niu and Meech, 2000), the physiological roles of KNa currents during normal patterns of neuronal activity remain poorly understood in part because of the absence of suitably selective pharmacological tools and also the complexities than can arise from manipulations of Na+.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Kameyama et al., 1984; Niu and Meech, 2000).

claim: The physiological roles of KNa currents during normal patterns of neuronal activity remain poorly understood.
source: Yet, despite apparently wide-spread expression both in neurons (Bhattacharjee et al., 2002, 2005) and other cells (Kameyama et al., 1984; Niu and Meech, 2000), the physiological roles of KNa currents during normal patterns of neuronal activity remain poorly understood in part because of the absence of suitably selective pharmacological tools and also the complexities than can arise from manipulations of Na+.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: The absence of suitably selective pharmacological tools contributes to poor understanding of KNa current physiological roles.
source: Yet, despite apparently wide-spread expression both in neurons (Bhattacharjee et al., 2002, 2005) and other cells (Kameyama et al., 1984; Niu and Meech, 2000), the physiological roles of KNa currents during normal patterns of neuronal activity remain poorly understood in part because of the absence of suitably selective pharmacological tools and also the complexities than can arise from manipulations of Na+.
evidence: This is an inference about methodological limitations in the field.

claim: KNa currents have been proposed to influence repetitive firing.
source: Because of potential coupling of KNa activation to Na+ influx through voltage-dependent Na+ (Nav) channels, KNa currents have been proposed to influence repetitive firing (Yang et al., 2007; Gribkoff and Kaczmarek, 2009) and postexcitatory afterhyperpolarizations (Franceschetti et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Yang et al., 2007; Gribkoff and Kaczmarek, 2009).

claim: KNa currents have been proposed to influence postexcitatory afterhyperpolarizations.
source: Because of potential coupling of KNa activation to Na+ influx through voltage-dependent Na+ (Nav) channels, KNa currents have been proposed to influence repetitive firing (Yang et al., 2007; Gribkoff and Kaczmarek, 2009) and postexcitatory afterhyperpolarizations (Franceschetti et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Franceschetti et al., 2003; Gao et al., 2008).

claim: KNa currents may be selectively activated by Na+ influx through Nav channel openings that persist at steady state following inactivation.
source: Recently, it has been suggested that KNa currents may be selectively activated by Na+ influx through Nav channel openings that persist at steady state following inactivation (Hage and Salkoff, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Hage and Salkoff, 2012).

claim: The authors genetically disrupted Kcnt1 and Kcnt2 genes to generate mouse strains lacking Slo2.1, Slo2.2, or both subunits.
source: To further probe the role of KNa currents, we have genetically disrupted Kcnt1 and Kcnt2 genes to generate mouse strains in which Slo2.1, Slo2.2, or both subunits together (Slo2 dKO) have been deleted.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Previous work has suggested an important role of Slo2 channels in sensory neurons.
source: Because previous work has suggested an important role of Slo2 channels in sensory neurons (Gao et al., 2008; Nuwer et al., 2010; Biton et al., 2012), we examined the consequences of KNa KO on sensory function and dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neuron excitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Gao et al., 2008; Nuwer et al., 2010; Biton et al., 2012).

claim: Slo2.2 channels play a role in acute itch sensation.
source: The results reveal a role of Slo2.2 channels in acute itch sensation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pruritic stimuli trigger an immediate increase in itch response in Slo2.2 KO mice.
source: Pruritic stimuli trigger an immediate increase in itch response in Slo2.2 KO mice, with later time points indistinguishable from WT animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At later time points after pruritic stimuli, itch responses in Slo2.2 KO mice are indistinguishable from WT animals.
source: Pruritic stimuli trigger an immediate increase in itch response in Slo2.2 KO mice, with later time points indistinguishable from WT animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: KO of Slo2.2, but not Slo2.1, abolishes KNa current in all small-diameter DRG neurons examined.
source: Furthermore, KO of Slo2.2, but not Slo2.1, removes a KNa current from all small-diameter DRG neurons examined.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by electrophysiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Small diameter neurons immunoreactive for isolectin B4 (IB4+) are enriched in neurons responsive to itch and pain stimuli.
source: To examine effects of Slo2 KO on DRG excitability, we focused on small diameter neurons, immunoreactive for isolectin Β4 (IB4+), which are known to be enriched in neurons responsive to itch and pain stimuli (Lallemend and Ernfors, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Lallemend and Ernfors, 2012).

claim: Slo2 KO increases firing frequency at any level of current injection in IB4+ DRG neurons.
source: Slo2 KO increases firing frequency at any level of current injection, while decreasing both rheobase and action potential (AP) threshold.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by electrophysiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Slo2 KO decreases rheobase in IB4+ DRG neurons.
source: Slo2 KO increases firing frequency at any level of current injection, while decreasing both rheobase and action potential (AP) threshold.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by electrophysiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Slo2 KO decreases action potential threshold in IB4+ DRG neurons.
source: Slo2 KO increases firing frequency at any level of current injection, while decreasing both rheobase and action potential (AP) threshold.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by electrophysiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of KNa acts as a brake to initiation of the first depolarization-elicited AP.
source: Activation of KNa acts as a brake to initiation of the first depolarization-elicited AP with no discernible effect on afterhyperpolarizations.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, based on electrophysiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: KNa activation has no discernible effect on afterhyperpolarizations in IB4+ DRG neurons.
source: Activation of KNa acts as a brake to initiation of the first depolarization-elicited AP with no discernible effect on afterhyperpolarizations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by electrophysiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Slo2.1 KO mice were generated via homologous recombination targeting exon 22 of the Kcnt2 gene.
source: Slo2.1 (gene: Kcnt2) and Slo2.2 (gene: Kcnt1) KO mice were generated via homologous recombination of specific targeting DNA fragments (Figure 1A,D) into the genome of mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells with confirmation by Southern blot (Figure 1B,E), generation of chimeric mice following injection of recombinant ES cells into C57BL/6 blastocysts, and then ultimately Cre/loxP mediated deletion of the targeted exons.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used to generate the knockout mice, supported by Figure 1.

claim: Slo2.2 KO mice were generated via homologous recombination targeting exon 11 of the Kcnt1 gene.
source: Slo2.1 (gene: Kcnt2) and Slo2.2 (gene: Kcnt1) KO mice were generated via homologous recombination of specific targeting DNA fragments (Figure 1A,D) into the genome of mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells with confirmation by Southern blot (Figure 1B,E), generation of chimeric mice following injection of recombinant ES cells into C57BL/6 blastocysts, and then ultimately Cre/loxP mediated deletion of the targeted exons.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used to generate the knockout mice, supported by Figure 1.

claim: Successful incorporation of the mutant allele into mice was confirmed by PCR genotyping of genomic DNA extracted from mouse tails.
source: Successful incorporation of the mutant allele into mice was confirmed by PCR genotyping of genomic DNA extracted from mouse tails (Figure 1C,F).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used to validate the knockout mice, supported by Figure 1C,F.

claim: The absence of specific native Slo2 protein was confirmed by western blots of total brain membrane proteins.
source: The absence of specific native Slo2 protein was confirmed by western blots of total brain membrane proteins (Figure 2; See 'Materials and methods' for discussion of Slo2 epitopes identified by antibodies).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental validation of the knockout mice, supported by Figure 2.

claim: Slo2.1 and Slo2.2 coassemble in WT brain.
source: Enrichment of brain Slo2 protein via sequential co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) and western blot further validated the successful KO of Slo2 proteins and also established that Slo2.1 and Slo2.2 coassemble in WT brain (Figure 2B–E), as indicated in earlier work (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by co-IP data in Figure 2B-E and a citation to earlier work (Chen et al., 2009).

claim: mRNAs encoding either Slo2.1 and Slo2.2 are broadly present in the central nervous system.
source: mRNAs encoding either Slo2.1 and Slo2.2 are broadly present in the central nervous system, with message for Slo2.1 notably more abundant in heart and aorta and message for Slo2.2 relatively enriched in other tissues including DRG and cerebellum.
evidence: This is a finding from the quantitative RT-PCR experiments presented in Figure 2F.

claim: Message for Slo2.1 is notably more abundant in heart and aorta.
source: mRNAs encoding either Slo2.1 and Slo2.2 are broadly present in the central nervous system, with message for Slo2.1 notably more abundant in heart and aorta and message for Slo2.2 relatively enriched in other tissues including DRG and cerebellum.
evidence: This is a finding from the quantitative RT-PCR experiments presented in Figure 2F.

claim: Message for Slo2.2 is relatively enriched in DRG and cerebellum.
source: mRNAs encoding either Slo2.1 and Slo2.2 are broadly present in the central nervous system, with message for Slo2.1 notably more abundant in heart and aorta and message for Slo2.2 relatively enriched in other tissues including DRG and cerebellum.
evidence: This is a finding from the quantitative RT-PCR experiments presented in Figure 2F.

claim: The selective expression of transcript for Slo2.1 in rat heart has been previously reported.
source: The selective expression of transcript for Slo2.1 in rat heart has been previously reported (Bhattacharjee et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Bhattacharjee et al., 2003).

claim: Slo2.1 protein was detected in DRG, spinal cord, cortex and heart.
source: Slo2.1 protein was detected in DRG, spinal cord, cortex and heart, but only a very weak band was seen from cerebellum (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a finding from the sequential IP and western blot experiments presented in Figure 2G.

claim: Only a very weak band of Slo2.1 protein was seen from cerebellum.
source: Slo2.1 protein was detected in DRG, spinal cord, cortex and heart, but only a very weak band was seen from cerebellum (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a finding from the sequential IP and western blot experiments presented in Figure 2G.

claim: Slo2.2 was observed in DRG, spinal cord, cortex, and cerebellum.
source: Slo2.2 was observed in DRG, spinal cord, cortex, and cerebellum, but not detectable in heart (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is a finding from the sequential IP and western blot experiments presented in Figure 2J.

claim: Slo2.2 was not detectable in heart.
source: Slo2.2 was observed in DRG, spinal cord, cortex, and cerebellum, but not detectable in heart (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is a finding from the sequential IP and western blot experiments presented in Figure 2J.

claim: Co-IP between Slo2.1 and Slo2.2 was observed in DRG, spinal cord, and cortex.
source: Co-IP between Slo2.1 and Slo2.2 was observed in those tissues for which both subunits were detectable: DRG, spinal cord, and cortex (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: This is a finding from the co-IP experiments presented in Figure 2H,I.

claim: KNa currents have been described in sensory neurons.
source: Because KNa currents have been described in sensory neurons (Gao et al., 2008; Tamsett et al., 2009; Nuwer et al., 2010), we chose DRG as a convenient system for investigation of potential physiological roles.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Gao et al., 2008; Tamsett et al., 2009; Nuwer et al., 2010).

claim: Single KO of either Slo2.1 or Slo2.2 did not influence the response latency in a 55°C hotplate test.
source: In a 55°C hotplate test, single KO of either Slo2.1 or Slo2.2 did not influence the response latency, although Slo2 dKO mice exhibited a briefer latency than WT mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Slo2 dKO mice exhibited a briefer latency than WT mice in a 55°C hotplate test.
source: In a 55°C hotplate test, single KO of either Slo2.1 or Slo2.2 did not influence the response latency, although Slo2 dKO mice exhibited a briefer latency than WT mice (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments presented in Figure 3A.

claim: No differences were observed between WT and Slo2 dKO mice in a formalin test.
source: In a formalin test, no differences were observed between WT and Slo2 dKO mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The absence of a difference in hotplate or formalin response in Slo2.2 KO mice agrees with recent observations on another Slo2.2 KO mouse.
source: The absence of a difference in hotplate or formalin response in Slo2.2 KO mice agrees with recent observations on another Slo2.2 KO mouse (Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study (Lu et al., 2015).

claim: Hindpaw injection of capsaicin elicits a characteristic licking behavior which was somewhat enhanced in Slo2 dKO mice.
source: Hindpaw injection of capsaicin elicits a characteristic licking behavior which was somewhat enhanced in Slo2 dKO mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Pronounced differences between WT and Slo2 dKO mice in capsaicin response were present at doses in excess of 0.0001 μg up through 0.01 μg.
source: Consistent with this idea, pronounced differences between WT and Slo2 dKO mice were present at doses in excess of 0.0001 μg up through 0.01 μg, with weaker differences at 0.03, 0.1 μg, and higher concentrations.
evidence: This is a finding from the dose-response experiments presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Weaker differences in capsaicin response between WT and Slo2 dKO mice were observed at 0.03, 0.1 μg, and higher concentrations.
source: Consistent with this idea, pronounced differences between WT and Slo2 dKO mice were present at doses in excess of 0.0001 μg up through 0.01 μg, with weaker differences at 0.03, 0.1 μg, and higher concentrations.
evidence: This is a finding from the dose-response experiments presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Mice lacking both Slo2.1 and Slo2.2 channels exhibit an enhanced aversion to moderate doses of capsaicin.
source: These results indicate that mice lacking both Slo2.1 and Slo2.2 channels exhibit an enhanced aversion to moderate doses of capsaicin and that Slo2 dKO can influence the acute response to sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dose-response data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Slo2 dKO can influence the acute response to sensory stimuli.
source: These results indicate that mice lacking both Slo2.1 and Slo2.2 channels exhibit an enhanced aversion to moderate doses of capsaicin and that Slo2 dKO can influence the acute response to sensory stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Chloroquine elicited robust enhancement of scratching behavior in Slo2 dKO mice during the first 5 min following injection.
source: Chloroquine (CQ, Figure 4A–F), histamine (HA, Figure 4G–L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E), and compound 48–80 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) elicited robust enhancement of scratching behavior in Slo2 dKO mice (Video 1 for the case of CQ), but not WT mice (Video 2), during the first 5 min following injection.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments presented in Figure 4A-F and Video 1.

claim: Histamine elicited robust enhancement of scratching behavior in Slo2 dKO mice during the first 5 min following injection.
source: Chloroquine (CQ, Figure 4A–F), histamine (HA, Figure 4G–L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E), and compound 48–80 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) elicited robust enhancement of scratching behavior in Slo2 dKO mice (Video 1 for the case of CQ), but not WT mice (Video 2), during the first 5 min following injection.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments presented in Figure 4G-L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: Compound 48-80 elicited robust enhancement of scratching behavior in Slo2 dKO mice during the first 5 min following injection.
source: Chloroquine (CQ, Figure 4A–F), histamine (HA, Figure 4G–L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E), and compound 48–80 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) elicited robust enhancement of scratching behavior in Slo2 dKO mice (Video 1 for the case of CQ), but not WT mice (Video 2), during the first 5 min following injection.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: No difference in itch behavior was observed between WT and Slo2 dKO mice after the first 5 min following pruritic injection.
source: No difference in itch behavior was observed between WT and Slo2 dKO mice after the first 5 min.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments presented in Figure 4.

claim: KO of only Slo2.2 resulted in enhanced itch response during the first 5 min after chloroquine injection.
source: KO of only Slo2.2 also revealed a similar alteration in the itch phenotype during the first 5 min after injection (CQ: Figure 4C,D; HA: Figure 4I,J).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments presented in Figure 4C,D.

claim: KO of only Slo2.2 resulted in enhanced itch response during the first 5 min after histamine injection.
source: KO of only Slo2.2 also revealed a similar alteration in the itch phenotype during the first 5 min after injection (CQ: Figure 4C,D; HA: Figure 4I,J).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments presented in Figure 4I,J.

claim: The enhanced itch response was also observed in heterozygous Slo2.2 mice.
source: The enhanced itch was also observed in heterozygous Slo2.2 mice.
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments presented in Figure 4D,J.

claim: WT and Slo2.1 mice exhibited no difference in response to chloroquine.
source: In contrast, WT and Slo2.1 mice exhibited no difference in response to either CQ (Figure 4E,F) or HA (Figure 4K,L).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments presented in Figure 4E,F.

claim: WT and Slo2.1 mice exhibited no difference in response to histamine.
source: In contrast, WT and Slo2.1 mice exhibited no difference in response to either CQ (Figure 4E,F) or HA (Figure 4K,L).
evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral experiments presented in Figure 4K,L.

claim: Sensory neurons contain a rich variety of K+ currents.
source: Sensory neurons contain a rich variety of K+ currents (Vydyanathan et al., 2005; Dobler et al., 2007; Li et al., 2007; Cho et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2010b; Liu et al., 2013) that complicate unambiguous definition of KNa current, for which selective pharmacological tools are lacking.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Vydyanathan et al., 2005; Dobler et al., 2007; Li et al., 2007; Cho et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2010b; Liu et al., 2013).

claim: Selective pharmacological tools for KNa current are lacking.
source: Sensory neurons contain a rich variety of K+ currents (Vydyanathan et al., 2005; Dobler et al., 2007; Li et al., 2007; Cho et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2010b; Liu et al., 2013) that complicate unambiguous definition of KNa current, for which selective pharmacological tools are lacking.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of available research tools.

claim: With 0 mM pipette Na+, little background current is observed with voltage-steps from −80 to −120 mV.
source: With 0 mM pipette Na+, little background current is observed with voltage-steps from −80 to −120 mV (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6A,C.

claim: With 70 mM pipette Na+, net current elicited by voltage-steps from −80 to −120 mV gradually increases over 3 min reaching a plateau near 1 nA.
source: With 70 mM pipette Na+, net current elicited by the same voltage-step gradually increases over 3 min reaching a plateau near 1 nA (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6A,C.

claim: Current activated by 70 mM pipette Na+ gradually diminishes at longer times following whole-cell access.
source: At longer times following whole-cell access, current activated by 70 mM pipette Na+ gradually diminishes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) despite no change in voltage-dependent Na+ current.
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The KNa current is blocked by extracellular 20 mM Cs+.
source: As in rat DRG neurons (Bischoff et al., 1998), the KNa current is blocked by extracellular 20 mM Cs+, with stronger inhibition at −120 mV than −80 mV reflecting the voltage-dependence of Cs+ inhibition (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and is consistent with prior work (Bischoff et al., 1998).

claim: Cs+ inhibition of KNa current is stronger at −120 mV than −80 mV, reflecting the voltage-dependence of Cs+ inhibition.
source: As in rat DRG neurons (Bischoff et al., 1998), the KNa current is blocked by extracellular 20 mM Cs+, with stronger inhibition at −120 mV than −80 mV reflecting the voltage-dependence of Cs+ inhibition (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The average amplitude of KNa current was similar for WT and Slo2.1 KO DRG neurons.
source: The average amplitude of KNa current was similar for WT and Slo2.1 KO DRG neurons (Figure 6B,C), while there was no KNa current in Slo2.2 KO or Slo2 dKO neurons (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6B,C.

claim: There was no KNa current in Slo2.2 KO or Slo2 dKO neurons.
source: The average amplitude of KNa current was similar for WT and Slo2.1 KO DRG neurons (Figure 6B,C), while there was no KNa current in Slo2.2 KO or Slo2 dKO neurons (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Excised inside-out patches confirmed that Slo2 dKO removed a Na-dependent K+ channel.
source: Excised inside-out patches confirmed that Slo2 dKO removed a Na–dependent K+ channel (Figure 6E) which exhibited little voltage-dependence over the range of −80 through −20 mV (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A) with a single channel conductance of about 127 pS (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6E.

claim: The Na-dependent K+ channel exhibited little voltage-dependence over the range of −80 through −20 mV.
source: Excised inside-out patches confirmed that Slo2 dKO removed a Na–dependent K+ channel (Figure 6E) which exhibited little voltage-dependence over the range of −80 through −20 mV (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A) with a single channel conductance of about 127 pS (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The Na-dependent K+ channel has a single channel conductance of about 127 pS.
source: Excised inside-out patches confirmed that Slo2 dKO removed a Na–dependent K+ channel (Figure 6E) which exhibited little voltage-dependence over the range of −80 through −20 mV (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A) with a single channel conductance of about 127 pS (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The average KNa background current with 70 mM pipette Na+ in IB4+ neurons did not differ significantly from that in IB4− neurons.
source: In WT DRG neurons, the average KNa background current with 70 mM pipette Na+ in IB4+ neurons did not differ significantly from that in IB4− neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Essentially all dissociated small diameter DRG neurons express KNa current which can be attributed exclusively to Slo2.2 subunits.
source: Our results suggest that essentially all dissociated small diameter DRG neurons express KNa current which can be attributed exclusively to Slo2.2 subunits.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiological data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The magnitude of the KNa current decreased with time in culture.
source: The magnitude of the KNa current decreased with time in culture, being ∼1013 ± 95 pA (n = 44 cells) after 2–10 hr of culture, but only 277 ± 70 pA (n = 9 cells) after 2–3 days in culture (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Slo2.2 accounted for most of the KNa current in DRG neurons in slices.
source: Measurement of KNa current in a set of small diameter neurons in DRG slices yielded similar results (Figure 6—figure supplement 5). However, one difference was that, although Slo2.2 accounted for most of the KNa current in DRG neurons in slices, after 2–3 min of dialysis of the pipette solution into the Slo2.2 KO neurons, some residual Na+-dependent current was observed.
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: After 2-3 min of dialysis of the pipette solution into the Slo2.2 KO neurons in slices, some residual Na+-dependent current was observed.
source: Measurement of KNa current in a set of small diameter neurons in DRG slices yielded similar results (Figure 6—figure supplement 5). However, one difference was that, although Slo2.2 accounted for most of the KNa current in DRG neurons in slices, after 2–3 min of dialysis of the pipette solution into the Slo2.2 KO neurons, some residual Na+-dependent current was observed.
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: Channels containing Slo2.1 subunits may be present at more peripheral locations in the DRG neurons.
source: Although neurons in slices may be uniquely affected by dialysis of 70 mM cytosolic Na+, this observation raises the possibility that channels containing Slo2.1 subunits may be present at more peripheral locations in the DRG neurons, perhaps consistent with the presence of message encoding Slo2.1 and some Slo2.1 protein in DRG samples, as described above.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data from DRG slices.

claim: Small diameter DRG neurons exhibit a complex range of electrical properties reflecting a rich variety of Nav and Kv channels.
source: Small diameter DRG neurons exhibit a complex range of electrical properties reflecting a rich variety of Nav (Vijayaragavan et al., 2001; Ho and O'Leary, 2011) and Kv channels (Zhang et al., 2010b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Vijayaragavan et al., 2001; Ho and O'Leary, 2011; Zhang et al., 2010b).

claim: Small diameter DRG neurons are heterogeneous in regards to sensitivity to various chemical signals.
source: Such neurons are also heterogeneous (Petruska et al., 2000; Dirajlal et al., 2003) in regards to sensitivity to various chemical signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Petruska et al., 2000; Dirajlal et al., 2003).

claim: AP firing was, on average, more robustly elevated in Slo2 dKO neurons than in WT neurons for identical amounts of injected current.
source: Despite considerable variability in the maximum firing rates among both WT and Slo2 dKO neurons, AP firing was, on average, more robustly elevated in Slo2 dKO neurons than in WT neurons for identical amounts of injected current (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 7C,D.

claim: The increase in firing in Slo2 dKO neurons was observed at all levels of current injection, both with 10 and 0 mM pipette Na+.
source: The increase in firing in Slo2 dKO neurons was observed at all levels of current injection, both with 10 and 0 mM pipette Na+ (Figure 7E–G).
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 7E-G.

claim: AP firing did not differ between 10 and 0 mM pipette Na+ within WT neurons or within Slo2 dKO neurons.
source: AP firing did not differ between 10 and 0 mM pipette Na+ within WT neurons or within Slo2 dKO neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from the electrophysiological experiments presented in Figure 7E-G.

claim: The increase in AP firing associated with KNa loss is consistent with increased AP firing of embryonic (E15) rat DRG neurons following protein kinase A-mediated internalization of KNa channels.
source: The increase in AP firing associated with KNa loss is consistent with increased AP firing of embryonic (E15) rat DRG neurons following protein kinase A-mediated internalization of KNa channels (Nuwer et al., 2010).

claim: Both at 10 and 0 mM Na+, less current was required to elicit an AP in the dKO neurons.

claim: The difference in excitability between the WT and dKO neurons arises from the absence of the KNa current itself.

claim: Direct evidence supporting the existence of KNa channels in native cells first appeared about 25–30 years ago.

claim: Full definition of functional properties and physiological roles of KNa currents have proven somewhat elusive.
source: Yet, even with identification of the two mammalian Slo2 genes that encode KNa channels of the type observed in the early studies (Bhattacharjee et al., 2003; Yuan et al., 2003), full definition of functional properties and physiological roles of KNa currents have proven somewhat elusive, despite the apparently widespread distribution of Slo2 subunits in excitable tissue (Bhattacharjee et al., 2002, 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Neurological disorders are linked to Slo2.2.
source: Recent demonstration of neurological disorders linked to Slo2.2 (Barcia et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2014) further highlights the potential importance of such channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies (Barcia et al., 2012; Martin et al., 2014).

claim: The present results confirm and extend earlier work regarding the loci of expression of Slo2 subunits.
source: The present results demonstrating the loci of expression of message for Slo2.1 and Slo2.2 subunits, the presence of Slo2.1 and Slo2.2 protein in various tissues, and the natural occurrence of Slo2.1/Slo2.2 heteromultimers confirms and extends earlier work regarding the loci of expression of Slo2 subunits (Bhattacharjee et al., 2002, 2003; Chen et al., 2009; Tamsett et al., 2009), while also providing KO controls confirming the utility of antibodies in western blots.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the present study, supported by citations to earlier work (Bhattacharjee et al., 2002, 2003; Chen et al., 2009; Tamsett et al., 2009).

claim: Slo2.2, but not Slo2.1, KO results in enhanced itch and, to a lesser extent, pain responses.
source: Here, focusing on the role of Slo2.2 in sensory function, we observed that Slo2.2, but not Slo2.1, KO results in enhanced itch and, to a lesser extent, pain responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Slo2 current results in increased excitability in response to depolarizing stimuli, likely accounting for the observed phenotypes.
source: Furthermore, KO of Slo2.2, but not Slo2.1, results in complete absence of the DRG KNa current. This loss of Slo2 current results in increased excitability in response to depolarizing stimuli, likely accounting for the observed phenotypes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiological data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The primary effect of KNa removal is to reduce AP threshold, with little or no clear effect on AHPs following an AP.
source: An important point of the present results is that the primary effect of KNa removal is to reduce AP threshold, with little or no clear effect on AHPs following an AP.

claim: The effect on AP threshold was revealed in multiple kinds of tests: a decrease in rheobase, a negative shift in AP threshold determined from the rate of AP rise (dV/dt), and a similar negative shift in the voltage at which current becomes net inward during a ramp protocol.
source: The effect on AP threshold was revealed in multiple kinds of tests, a decrease in rheobase, a negative shift in AP threshold determined from the rate of AP rise (dV/dt), and also from a similar negative shift in the voltage at which current becomes net inward during a ramp protocol.
evidence: This is a summary of the electrophysiological findings presented in Figure 8 and Figure 9.

claim: No difference in AHP amplitude was observed following single APs between WT and KO cells, either with 0 or 10 mM pipette Na+.
source: Furthermore, we observed no difference in AHP amplitude measured following single APs between WT and KO cells, either with 0 or 10 mM pipette Na+.

claim: A role of KNa activity preceding the AP upswing in DRG neurons differs fundamentally from other explanations of the proposed role of KNa current in other cells.
source: A role of KNa activity preceding the AP upswing in DRG neurons differs fundamentally from other explanations of the proposed role of KNa current in other cells.

claim: In different cases, a primary role for KNa current has been proposed either in fast or slower afterhyperpolarizations that may require trains of several APs to develop.
source: In different cases, a primary role for KNa current has been proposed either in fast (Hess et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2007; Gribkoff and Kaczmarek, 2009; Markham et al., 2013) or slower afterhyperpolarizations that may require trains of several APs to develop (Schwindt et al., 1989; Kim and McCormick, 1998; Franceschetti et al., 2003; Wallen et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2010a).

claim: The present results do not preclude such roles for KNa either in rapid repolarization or slow AHPs in other cells.
source: The present results do not preclude such roles for KNa either in rapid repolarization or slow AHPs in other cells.

claim: The specific role of KNa channels in any cell would depend intimately on the balance of other repolarizing conductances, along with magnitude, spatial, and temporal properties of any cytosolic [Na+] elevation.
source: However, the specific role of KNa channels in any cell would depend intimately on the balance of other repolarizing conductances, along with magnitude, spatial, and temporal properties of any cytosolic [Na+] elevation.

claim: In rat DRG neurons, both AP duration and AHPs were unchanged when extracellular Na+ was replaced by Li+.
source: Our observations are, in fact, consistent with earlier results in rat DRG neurons, in which both AP duration and AHPs were unchanged when extracellular Na+ was replaced by Li+ (Bischoff et al., 1998), despite the fact that Li+ does not substitute for Na+ in KNa activation (Safronov and Vogel, 1996).

claim: Li+ does not substitute for Na+ in KNa activation.

claim: Consideration of basic properties of Na+ diffusion and the expected Na+ flux through single channels have raised some doubt whether average [Na+]i can ever be sufficient to activate KNa.

claim: The threshold for KNa activation may be higher than 10 mM.

claim: Regulation of KNa current may have more impact on weaker stimuli or relatively weak depolarizing drive.
